name: Semiclosed World, the Bag of Gold
description: More than half of a closed Friedmann universe of dust joined to Schwarzschild's exterior behind its throat. The mass seen from outside falls as the dust within grows, and reaches zero as the universe closes.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit, and $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ is the Schwarzschild radius of the mass seen from outside. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: How much can you hide behind a given mass? J. Robert Oppenheimer and Hartland Snyder built their collapsing star in 1939 by cutting a ball out of a closed universe of dust and setting Schwarzschild's vacuum around it [oppenheimersnyder1939]. The closed universe is a three sphere, so the ball is everything within an angle $\chi_0$ of its centre, and for a star $\chi_0$ stays below $\pi/2$, short of the equator [hsu2008unitarity]. Now keep cutting past the equator. Each new layer adds dust to the ball while the sphere that bounds it shrinks, and the mass an outsider measures, $M = (c^2/2G)\,a_m\sin^3\chi_0$ for a universe of greatest radius $a_m$, goes down [hsu2008unitarity]. At $\chi_0 = \pi$ the ball is the whole universe, and the mass is zero [hsu2008unitarity].¶Such a ball is called a semiclosed world [zelmanov1965]. Yakov Zel'dovich and, independently, Igor Novikov studied it in 1962 and 1963: more than half of a Friedmann universe, in the words of A. L. Zelmanov's report on Soviet cosmology to the International Astronomical Union, "connected with the outer space through a narrow neck" [zelmanov1965]. The neck is the throat of Schwarzschild's geometry, and the dust sits behind it, on the second sheet of space, where the spheres grow again as you walk away from the outside world [hsu2008unitarity]. These models show, Zelmanov wrote, that adding a spherical layer of matter can lower the gravitational mass of a sphere, "because of the increased gravitational mass-defect" [zelmanov1965]. Novikov went on in 1964 to explore what he called R regions, where the radius of the spheres can serve as a coordinate of space, and T regions, where it can only be a time, and to define the comoving coordinates of Schwarzschild's solution that carry his name [novikov1964, krasinski2001novikov].¶At the Les Houches summer school of 1963, John Archibald Wheeler lectured on the initial value problem: choose the geometry of one moment of time, subject to Einstein's constraints, and let the equations carry it forward [wheeler1964, marolf2009]. In those lectures he sewed a large closed universe onto the back of Schwarzschild's bridge, with his attention on the universe side of it [marolf2009]. He also used the phrase "bag of gold" there, for another thing: a part of space pinched off, singularly, where the conformal factor of his method passed through zero [marolf2009]. The name has since moved to the universe behind the throat, where Donald Marolf found it in "frequent though informal use" [marolf2009].¶What would you see from outside? A black hole of mass $M$, and no sign of what is behind it [hsu2008unitarity]. The usual picture, a sphere hanging from a funnel, is a single moment, the instant of greatest expansion [marolf2009]. Before it the dust came out of a bang, and after it the dust falls back into a crunch behind the horizon [hsu2008unitarity]. Robert Fuller and Wheeler had found in 1962 that Schwarzschild's bridge pinches off faster than light can cross it, and the throat of the bag is that bridge [fuller1962, marolf2009]. Run the film backward from that moment and the same collapse plays in reverse, so a bag left to itself must have come out of a white hole, and Stephen Hsu and David Reeb add that no laboratory, however advanced, could build one [hsu2008unitarity].¶Add an electric charge and the world can no longer close. Moissei Markov and Valeri Frolov found in 1970 that for any charge, however small, the nearly closed Friedmann universe opens through a narrow throat into the Reissner-Nordström exterior [markov1970]. They called such objects electromagnetic friedmons [markov1970]. Twenty years on, Frolov, Markov, and Viatcheslav Mukhanov put a closed world where the singularity of a black hole would be: if curvature has an upper limit, they argued, Schwarzschild's interior can pass into a de Sitter universe [frolov1990closed].¶The entropy that Jacob Bekenstein and Stephen Hawking gave a black hole is a quarter of the area of its horizon in Planck units, and $M$ fixes that area [bekenstein1973, hawking1975, hsu2008monsters]. The bag behind the throat, at the same $M$, can be as large as you like and hold as much as you like [marolf2009]. So what does the area count? Hsu and Reeb set the bag beside their monsters, balls of matter with more entropy than a black hole of equal mass, and concluded that a unitary theory of quantum gravity has to leave most such configurations out [hsu2008monsters, hsu2008unitarity]. Marolf argued in 2009 that in the duality between anti-de Sitter space and conformal field theory the entropy counts the states that can be told apart from outside, with the bags in sectors of their own [marolf2009]. Joydeep Chakravarty proposed in 2021 that the interior states are fewer than they look, since excitations that seem orthogonal overlap slightly [chakravarty2021].

related.text: The same cut of a closed universe of dust taken short of the equator, $\chi_0 < \pi/2$. There the surface faces the outside directly, and the dust is a star that collapses [oppenheimersnyder1939].
The inside of the bag: the ball $\chi \le \chi_0$ of a closed Friedmann universe of dust, more than half of it, from its bang to its crunch.
The outside, entered from behind. The surface of the dust lies on the second sheet of the extended solution, with the throat between it and the observer who measures the mass [hsu2008unitarity].

The throat the bag hangs by. Einstein and Rosen's bridge joins two sheets of Schwarzschild's exterior, and here the second sheet ends at the surface of the dust and is closed with a universe [marolf2009].

Dust whose density and energy vary from shell to shell. The semiclosed world is uniform dust inside $\chi_0$ and none outside, and the throat Novikov discussed is what later authors named the neck of a Tolman-Bondi model [krasinski2001novikov].
The outside of the charged version. Markov and Frolov found that a closed universe of charged dust cannot close, and opens through a narrow throat into this exterior [markov1970].
Other moments of time symmetry, with several throats and no dust. Wheeler's own bag of gold was a piece of such a moment, pinched off where the conformal factor passes through zero [marolf2009].

A moment of time symmetry with no dust and no throat to begin with, only gravitational waves. Turned up to its critical amplitude the wave closes its slice into a compact universe of its own [omurchadha1993].

coordinates.name: Comoving Dust Interior

parameters.description: Scale factor of the dust, a length ($a > 0$), obeying $2a\ddot{a}+\dot{a}^2+1 = 0$

Comoving polar angle of the surface of the dust ($\pi/2 < \chi_0 < \pi$), past the equator of the three sphere, fixed by $\sin^2\chi_0 = r_s/R_0$ with $R_0 = a_m\sin\chi_0$ the greatest areal radius of the surface
Scale factor at the moment of greatest expansion, the radius of the three sphere the dust is cut from, tied to the exterior mass by $r_s = a_m\sin^3\chi_0$

coordinates.convention: We use comoving coordinates $(\tau, \chi, \theta, \phi)$, where $\tau$ is the proper time of the dust, zero at the moment of greatest expansion, $\chi$ is a dimensionless comoving polar angle, and the scale factor $a(\tau)$ carries the length. The dust begins and ends at $a = 0$, at $\tau = \mp\tau_s$ with $\tau_s = \dfrac{\pi a_m}{2c}$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = c\tau$, a dot on the scale factor is $\dot{a} = \dfrac{1}{c}\dfrac{da}{d\tau}$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{\tau}$ means $d(c\tau)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{\tau} + a\,\partial_\tau a\,\dot{\chi}^2 + a\,\partial_\tau a\,\sin^2\chi\,\dot{\theta}^2 + a\,\partial_\tau a\,\sin^2\chi\sin^2\theta\,\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Conformal Dust Interior

parameters.description: Scale factor at the moment of greatest expansion, the radius of the three sphere the dust is cut from, tied to the exterior mass by $r_s = a_m\sin^3\chi_0$

Comoving polar angle of the surface of the dust ($\pi/2 < \chi_0 < \pi$), past the equator of the three sphere, fixed by $\sin^2\chi_0 = r_s/R_0$ with $R_0 = a_m\sin\chi_0$ the greatest areal radius of the surface

coordinates.convention: We use the conformal time $\eta$ of the dust, a dimensionless angle with $a\,d\eta = c\,d\tau$ for its proper time $\tau$, and the comoving polar angle $\chi$. The scale factor is $a = \tfrac{1}{2}a_m(1 + \cos\eta)$, greatest at $\eta = 0$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Schwarzschild Exterior
domains: r \le R(t) \;\text{(on the sheet of the dust)}

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the mass a distant observer measures, $r_s = 2GM/c^2 = a_m\sin^3\chi_0$

coordinates.convention: We use Schwarzschild coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ on either sheet of the exterior, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $t = 0$ at the moment of greatest expansion, and $R(t)$ is the areal radius of the surface of the dust. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Isotropic Exterior

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the mass a distant observer measures, $r_s = 2GM/c^2 = a_m\sin^3\chi_0$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the isotropic radius, so the areal radius is $r(1 + r_s/4r)^2$, and $r_d(t)$ is the isotropic radius of the surface of the dust. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{r} + \dfrac{2048r^4\,r_s\left(4r - r_s\right)}{\left(4r + r_s\right)^7}\dot{t}^2 - \dfrac{2r_s}{r\left(4r + r_s\right)}\dot{r}^2 - \dfrac{r\left(4r - r_s\right)}{4r + r_s}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{r\left(4r - r_s\right)\sin^2\theta}{4r + r_s}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0
